cPanel LiteSpeed plugin root privesc: generateEcCert->packageUserSize API chain/burst (CVE-2026-54420) AIExploitation High
Hunts the in-the-wild exploitation pattern for CVE-2026-54420 in cPanel access logs: the LiteSpeed plugin cert-generation API (cpanel_jsonapi_func=generateEcCert) chained immediately with packageUserSize for the same user, and/or 7-10 concurrent cert API calls in one burst. Legitimate WHM/cPanel UI flows call these one at a time and never chain them, so the chain or the burst is the high-fidelity exploitation signal. Rationale: Anchored on the exact vendor-published exploitation indicators (cpanel_jsonapi_func=generateEcCert, cpanel_jsonapi_func=packageUserSize, cert_action_entry geneccert) plus the two false-positive-rule-outs LiteSpeed published: generateEcCert immediately followed by packageUserSize for the same user, and 7-10 concurrent calls per attempt. Corroborated against LiteSpeed's advisory, BleepingComputer and SecurityAffairs. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.litespeedtech.com/2026/06/01/security-update-for-litespeed-cpanel-plugin-2/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-warns-of-another-actively-exploited-cpanel-plugin-flaw/ • https://securityaffairs.com/193684/security/u-s-cisa-adds-cisco-catalyst-and-litespeed-cpanel-plugin-flaws-to-its-known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog.html
ATT&CKT1068
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Single generateEcCert call from the WHM/cPanel UI when a user manually issues an EC SSL certificate (no packageUserSize pairing, no burst)
  • cPanel AutoSSL renewal cycles generating multiple certs for many domains sequentially
  • A busy reseller/host admin issuing several certificates back-to-back during onboarding
  • Monitoring or provisioning automation that scripts cert issuance through the cPanel JSON API
  • Load/penetration testing of the cPanel API by the hosting provider
Suppression filter
// Sentinel: drop AutoSSL/system-driven cert issuance and keep only the chain or true burst
| where not (Funcs has "generateEcCert" and not (Funcs has "packageUserSize") and Calls < 7)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the offending account/user and src IP from the alert; confirm the generateEcCert+packageUserSize pairing or 7-10 call burst within the 2m window and check whether the source is an end-user FTP/web-shell account rather than the AutoSSL system context. 2) Contain: suspend the implicated cPanel account, kill its active sessions/FTP, and on the host verify CageFS integrity and check for new root-owned files or unexpected setuid binaries; isolate the server if root compromise is confirmed. 3) Hunt: confirm LiteSpeed cPanel plugin is upgraded to >=2.4.8 (WHM >=5.3.2.1); grep all cpanel logs for the indicators across every tenant on the box, review root cron/SSH keys/passwd changes since first-seen, and scope sibling shared-hosting nodes for the same call pattern.
// Assumes cPanel access logs (cpsrvd/access_log) are forwarded to the Syslog connector.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("generateEcCert","packageUserSize","geneccert")
| extend Func = case(SyslogMessage has "cpanel_jsonapi_func=generateEcCert","generateEcCert", SyslogMessage has "cpanel_jsonapi_func=packageUserSize","packageUserSize", SyslogMessage has "geneccert","geneccert","other")
| summarize Calls=count(), Funcs=make_set(Func), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), SampleMsg=any(SyslogMessage) by Computer, TimeBin=bin(TimeGenerated, 2m)
| where (Funcs has "generateEcCert" and Funcs has "packageUserSize") or Calls >= 7   // chain (legit UI never pairs these) OR burst (legit UI = 1 at a time)
| sort by Calls desc
source:linux.syslog ("cpanel_jsonapi_func=generateEcCert" OR "cpanel_jsonapi_func=packageUserSize" OR "geneccert")

Exposure hunt: hosts running vulnerable LiteSpeed cPanel plugin < 2.4.8 (CVE-2026-54420 KEV) AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces servers still exposed to CVE-2026-54420 so the CISA KEV remediation deadline (FCEB due 2026-06-18) can be tracked. Pivots on the vulnerability inventory rather than behaviour: any asset reporting CVE-2026-54420 (LiteSpeed cPanel plugin before 2.4.8 / WHM plugin before 5.3.2.0) is unpatched and root-privesc-exploitable. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE id (CVE-2026-54420) and the vendor-stated fixed version (cPanel plugin 2.4.8 / WHM 5.3.2.1) to enumerate unpatched assets ahead of the CISA KEV deadline; high precision because it keys on the assigned CVE rather than a guessed software string. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.litespeedtech.com/2026/06/01/security-update-for-litespeed-cpanel-plugin-2/ • https://securityaffairs.com/193684/security/u-s-cisa-adds-cisco-catalyst-and-litespeed-cpanel-plugin-flaws-to-its-known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog.html
ATT&CKT1068
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Asset already patched to 2.4.8/5.3.2.1 but scanner cache is stale and still reports the CVE
  • Server runs the WHM plugin only without the bundled user-end cPanel plugin (vendor notes WHM plugin itself is not affected)
  • Decommissioned shared-hosting node still present in the asset inventory
  • Scanner version-detection false match on a backported/vendor-patched build that keeps the old version banner
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reported SoftwareVersion is genuinely below 2.4.8 (cPanel plugin) / 5.3.2.0 (WHM bundle) and that the user-end plugin (not just WHM) is installed. 2) Contain: schedule/apply the upgrade to LiteSpeed cPanel plugin 2.4.8 (WHM 5.3.2.1) immediately given active exploitation and KEV due date 2026-06-18; where patching is delayed, tighten FTP/web-shell account access and monitor with the behavioural UC. 3) Hunt: for every still-vulnerable host, run the generateEcCert/packageUserSize log grep to determine whether exploitation already occurred before patching, and confirm no root-level persistence was planted.

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"

      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files

DeviceEvents

| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Browser/Playwright process overwriting vite.config / vitest.config (CVE-2026-53633) AIInstallation High
Hunts the verified impact of CVE-2026-53633: a CDP-driven browser download writes attacker-controlled vite.config.ts into the project root, which Vitest then reloads as Node.js code. A Chromium/Playwright browser binary creating or modifying a build/test config file is essentially never legitimate, making this the highest-fidelity pivot for the exploit. Rationale: Keys on the exact verified impact chain in the GHSA: a CDP Page.setDownloadBehavior + Runtime.evaluate download writing vite.config.ts to project root, with a browser binary (incl. Playwright's headless_shell/chrome) as the writer. Excluding the user Downloads folder removes the only benign way a browser legitimately writes such a name. Cross-checked against the upstream vitest advisory and GitLab Advisory DB. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm • https://github.com/vitest-dev/vitest/security/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@vitest/browser/CVE-2026-53633/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team reproducing CVE-2026-53633 in a sandbox
  • Vitest's own browser-mode self-tests running in a CI image where the test harness is a browser
  • Developer doing browser 'Save As' of a file literally named vite.config.ts into a repo (mitigated by Downloads exclusion)
  • A browser-embedded local IDE/extension that persists project files through the renderer process
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains "ms-playwright" or FolderPath !contains "\\node_modules\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writer is a real browser/Playwright binary and the target is a tracked project config; diff the new vite.config content for require/child_process/exec/fetch or base64 blobs. 2) Contain: kill the Vitest watch (node) and browser sessions on the host, isolate the endpoint, and revert vite.config from version control. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for node.exe children spawned within 60s of the write (UC2), inbound connections to the Vitest listener (UC4), and any `--browser.api.host=0.0.0.0` invocations (UC3).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("vite.config.ts","vite.config.js","vite.config.mjs","vite.config.mts","vite.config.cjs","vitest.config.ts","vitest.config.js","vitest.config.mjs","vitest.config.mts")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","chromium.exe","headless_shell.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe")
| where FolderPath !contains "\\Downloads\\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FileOriginUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("vite.config.ts","vite.config.js","vite.config.mjs","vite.config.mts","vite.config.cjs","vitest.config.ts","vitest.config.js","vitest.config.mjs","vitest.config.mts")
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","chromium.exe","headless_shell.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe")
| where TargetFilePath !contains "\\Downloads\\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 6f3a1b2c-9d4e-4a77-bf21-7c1e5a9d0e11
description: A Chromium/Playwright browser binary writing a vite.config or vitest.config file indicates abuse of the Vitest Browser Mode CDP bridge (CVE-2026-53633) to overwrite project config and gain Node.js RCE.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm
  - https://github.com/vitest-dev/vitest/security/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm

  - attack.t1546

  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\chromium.exe'
      - '\headless_shell.exe'

Vitest config overwrite by browser followed by Node child execution (CVE-2026-53633 RCE) AIActions on Objectives High
Correlates the CVE-2026-53633 config overwrite with the resulting code execution: a browser binary writes vite.config/vitest.config, then the running Vitest node process spawns a child process within seconds as the reloaded, attacker-controlled config executes. The temporal link between a browser-written config and node-spawned children is the proof of RCE, not just exposure. Rationale: Joins the article's two-step chain — browser writes vite.config (CDP download) then 'Vitest reloads the changed config and executes attacker-controlled Node.js code' — by requiring a node/vitest-parented child process within 60s of a browser-written config on the same host. The browser-writer + node-parent combo within seconds is what separates exploitation from benign config edits. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm • https://github.com/vitest-dev/vitest/security/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm
ATT&CKT1546 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Vitest watch reload after a developer edits config in a browser-based local IDE
  • CVE reproduction/red-team exercise on a dev box
  • Vitest self-tests in CI that intentionally rewrite config during a run
  • A browser extension that round-trips project files then triggers a vite HMR reload
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "esbuild" and ProcessCommandLine !has "--version"
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the spawned child cmdline (DelaySec near 0 = automated) and the new config content for malicious Node payloads. 2) Contain: terminate the node/vitest watcher and child processes, isolate the host, restore config from VCS, and rotate any secrets reachable from the project (.env, npm tokens). 3) Hunt: enumerate outbound connections and files created by the child process, and sweep other dev endpoints for `--browser.api.host=0.0.0.0` Vitest listeners (UC3).
let LookbackDays = 30d;
let WindowSeconds = 60;
let ConfigWrites = DeviceFileEvents

    | where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","chromium.exe","headless_shell.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe")
    | project ConfigWriteTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, ConfigFile = FileName, ConfigPath = FolderPath, WriterProcess = InitiatingProcessFileName;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("vitest","vite")
| join kind=inner ConfigWrites on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (ConfigWriteTime .. ConfigWriteTime + WindowSeconds * 1s)
| project ConfigWriteTime, ReexecTime = Timestamp, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ConfigWriteTime), DeviceName, ConfigFile, ConfigPath, WriterProcess, ChildProcess = FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by ConfigWriteTime desc
let LookbackDays = 30d;
let WindowSeconds = 60;
let ConfigWrites = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where TargetFileName in~ ("vite.config.ts","vite.config.js","vite.config.mjs","vite.config.mts","vite.config.cjs","vitest.config.ts","vitest.config.js","vitest.config.mjs")
    | where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
    | where ActingProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","chromium.exe","headless_shell.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe")
    | project ConfigWriteTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ConfigFile = TargetFileName, WriterProcess = ActingProcessName;
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ParentProcessName has "node.exe"
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("vitest","vite")
| join kind=inner ConfigWrites on DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (ConfigWriteTime .. ConfigWriteTime + WindowSeconds * 1s)
| project ConfigWriteTime, ReexecTime = TimeGenerated, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, ConfigWriteTime), DvcHostname, ConfigFile, WriterProcess, ChildProcess = ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by ConfigWriteTime desc
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/node\.exe/i
| join({#event_simpleName=FileWritten | TargetFileName=/\\(vite|vitest)\.config\.(ts|js|mjs|mts|cjs)$/i | ContextImageFileName=/\\(chrome|chromium|headless_shell|msedge|firefox|brave)\.exe$/i}, field=aid, include=[TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, TargetFileName], function=count())

Vitest Browser Mode API exposed to all interfaces (--browser.api.host=0.0.0.0) AIDelivery Medium
Identifies the precise dangerous configuration enabling remote exploitation of CVE-2026-53633: a Vitest/node process started with the browser API bound to 0.0.0.0. The query also surfaces whether allowWrite/allowExec are disabled — the 'false sense of security' the advisory calls out, since CDP bypasses those flags regardless. Rationale: Uses the exact CLI string the advisory's Impact section names ('--browser.api.host=0.0.0.0') as the condition that turns the local CDP bypass into a remote RCE, and flags the allowWrite/allowExec=false combination the article explicitly calls out as a false sense of security. This is a posture hunt, hence hunting tier — it finds exposure, not confirmed compromise. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@vitest/browser/CVE-2026-53633/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CI/container runners intentionally binding 0.0.0.0 inside an isolated network
  • Developers running Vitest UI to share a test session with a teammate on the LAN
  • Cloud dev environments (Codespaces/Gitpod) that bind 0.0.0.0 by design
  • Security team validating the patched 3.2.5/4.1.8/5.0.0-beta.4 behavior
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !startswith "ci-" and DeviceName !startswith "runner-"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host runs a vulnerable @vitest/browser (>=3.0.0<=3.2.4, >=4.0.0<=4.1.7, 5.0.0-beta.0..3) or vite-plus<=0.1.23 and whether the API is reachable off-host. 2) Contain: stop the exposed Vitest watcher, restrict the API to 127.0.0.1, and upgrade to 3.2.5 / 4.1.8 / 5.0.0-beta.4+. 3) Hunt: check for inbound connections to the listener (UC4) and any browser-written config files (UC1) on this host during the exposure window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","vitest.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "vitest"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--browser.api.host=0.0.0.0","--browser.api.host 0.0.0.0","--api.host=0.0.0.0","--api.host 0.0.0.0")
| extend WriteExecDisabled = ProcessCommandLine has_any ("allowWrite=false","allowWrite false","allowExec=false","allowExec false")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, WriteExecDisabled, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","vitest.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "vitest"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--browser.api.host=0.0.0.0","--browser.api.host 0.0.0.0","--api.host=0.0.0.0","--api.host 0.0.0.0")
| extend WriteExecDisabled = ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("allowWrite=false","allowExec=false")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, WriteExecDisabled
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Remote inbound connection to Vitest Browser Mode listener (node, non-loopback) AIExploitation Medium
Detects a remote client reaching an exposed Vitest browser API: the node/vitest process accepts an inbound connection from a non-loopback address. Remote exploitation of CVE-2026-53633 requires connecting to the WebSocket API (default port 63315) to scrape the API token/session and issue CDP RPC, so a non-local inbound to the vitest listener is the network signature of the attack. Rationale: Pins the Defender query to the reliable signal (a vitest-cmdline node process accepting a non-loopback inbound), and uses the article's stated listener port 63315 where process attribution isn't available (Datadog/Falcon). Sentinel left empty because the standard ASIM/SecurityEvent tables in this tenant carry no inbound-connection record attributable to the listening node/vitest process — explained per the schema's process-attribution gap. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm • https://github.com/vitest-dev/vitest/security/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm
ATT&CKT1190 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Teammates on the LAN connecting to a shared Vitest UI / dev server
  • Mobile or VM browsers hitting the dev server for cross-device testing
  • Internal vulnerability scanners or asset-discovery probes touching the port
  • Monitoring/health-check agents connecting to the node listener
Suppression filter
| where RemoteIP !in ("<populate with known dev/monitoring subnets via watchlist>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the RemoteIP — is it a known dev/teammate host or unexpected/external? Correlate the connection time with any browser-written config (UC1) on the same host. 2) Contain: if unexpected, isolate the host, kill the Vitest watcher, and block the source IP; rebind the API to localhost. 3) Hunt: review the source IP's activity org-wide and check the target host for node-spawned child processes and new config files post-connection.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "vitest"
| where RemoteIPType !in ("Loopback","LinkLocal")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemoteIPType, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "vitest"
| where RemoteIPType !in ("Loopback","LinkLocal")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemoteIPType, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails

The Hacker News
2026-06-15 11 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email. The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message

INFINITERED trojanized REDCap web-shell files by known SHA256 AIInstallation Medium
Hunts INFINITERED, the custom PHP malware UNC6508 wrote into REDCap's own system files to harvest credentials and run a backdoor. Matches the seven GTIG-published file hashes on any endpoint where Defender/MDE-for-Linux file telemetry exists on the REDCap server. Rationale: Uses the seven GTIG-published INFINITERED SHA256 hashes — confirmed in the Google Cloud blog and the Google SecOps community YARA-L thread (second source) — so an exact hash match is true-positive by definition. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/prc-targets-us-medical-research • https://security.googlecloudcommunity.com/google-security-operations-2/custom-malware-named-infinitered-yara-l-rules-to-detect-unc6508-7744
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1554
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/EDR vendor downloading the sample to a malware-analysis sandbox host
  • DFIR analyst staging the IOC file on a forensic workstation for reversing
  • Backup/restore job re-writing a previously infected REDCap file from an old snapshot
  • AV quarantine engine copying the file into a quarantine vault (FolderPath shows AV path)
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has "\\Quarantine\\" and FolderPath !has "/quarantine/" and not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MpCmdRun.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is an externally-facing REDCap/PHP server vs an analysis/quarantine host (check FolderPath and DeviceName); a hit on a production REDCap server is a confirmed compromise. 2) Contain: isolate the server, rotate all REDCap DB/service-account credentials, and pull the `redcap_sessions` table for rows prefixed `xc32038474a` (stolen creds). 3) Hunt: search for inbound HTTP requests carrying the `REDCAP-TOKEN` cookie and any logon/admin activity from 23.169.65.49, then audit Google Workspace/M365 content-compliance and forwarding rules created after the compromise window (Sept 2023+).

UNC6508 admin-login / network activity from 23.169.65.49 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the attacker source IP GTIG attributed to UNC6508 — a compromised ASUS router used as an admin-login source against victim infrastructure. Fires on any authentication or network connection involving 23.169.65.49. Rationale: 23.169.65.49 is the single attacker IP in GTIG's IOC set, corroborated as an admin-login source from a compromised ASUS router (cybersecuritynews). A single confirmed-bad IP is a clean alerting pivot across auth and network telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/prc-targets-us-medical-research • https://cybersecuritynews.com/prc-nexus-hackers-exploit-redcap-servers/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1078
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • The IP is re-allocated/cleaned and later legitimately reused by an ISP customer (validate event date against Sept 2023–Nov 2025 activity window)
  • Threat-intel platform actively scanning/sinkholing the now-disabled infrastructure
  • Internal security tooling pinging the IOC for reachability checks
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine direction — inbound admin login (AADSignIn/Signin) vs outbound connection — and identify the account/host involved. 2) Contain: block the IP at perimeter, force-reset and re-MFA any account that authenticated from it, and revoke active sessions/tokens. 3) Hunt: pivot from the affected account to mailbox-rule changes, content-compliance rules, and REDCap server hashes; check for the REDCAP-TOKEN cookie traffic on web tier.

Mail content-compliance / transport rule blind-copying mail to an external address AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts UNC6508's headline exfiltration TTP — abusing a built-in domain mail rule to silently BCC keyword-matching mail to an attacker inbox. Expressed on M365 mail-flow (transport) rules, the direct equivalent of the Google Workspace content-compliance rule, by flagging New/Set-TransportRule operations that add a BlindCopyTo/RedirectMessageTo target. Rationale: The article's novel TTP is an org-level content-compliance rule (GTIG's words) that BCCs keyword-matching mail to an attacker Gmail; on M365 telemetry available in this tenant the exact analog is a transport rule with BlindCopyTo/RedirectMessageTo. Native Google Workspace detection uses the same logic on Admin SDK Reports API CREATE_GMAIL_SETTING / content-compliance events, not in the canonical schema, hence Splunk/Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left blank. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/prc-targets-us-medical-research • https://www.darkreading.com/threat-intelligence/china-nexus-actor-us-researchers-undetected
ATT&CKT1114.003 T1098.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate compliance/eDiscovery journaling rule BCC'ing a regulated archive mailbox
  • Security team routing a copy of suspicious mail to a phishing-analysis/abuse mailbox
  • Exec-assistant or shared-team workflow legitimately copying mail to an internal distribution list
  • MSP/migration tooling setting interim transport rules during a tenant cutover
Suppression filter
| where RuleTarget !has "@yourorg.com" and RuleTarget !has_any ("journal","archive","ediscovery","abuse@","phishing@")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the RuleTarget recipient — internal/known-archive is likely benign; an external/free-mail (gmail.com, outlook.com) destination is high-suspicion. Check the rule's match conditions for sensitive keyword lists. 2) Contain: disable/delete the rule, revoke the creating admin's sessions, and quarantine any mail already copied to the external address. 3) Hunt: review who/where the rule was created from (ClientIP vs 23.169.65.49), enumerate all transport + inbox forwarding rules tenant-wide, and confirm phishing-resistant MFA on all admin accounts.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in~ ("New-TransportRule","Set-TransportRule")
| extend Raw = parse_json(RawEventData)
| extend ParamsStr = tostring(Raw.Parameters)
| where ParamsStr has_any ("BlindCopyTo","RedirectMessageTo","AddToRecipients","CopyTo")
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, ActionType, ObjectName, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity

| where Operation in~ ("New-TransportRule","Set-TransportRule")
| extend Params = todynamic(Parameters)
| mv-apply p = Params on (
    where tostring(p.Name) in~ ("BlindCopyTo","RedirectMessageTo","AddToRecipients","CopyTo")
    | extend RuleTarget = tostring(p.Value)
  )
| where isnotempty(RuleTarget)
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, ClientIP, Operation, RuleTarget, Parameters
| order by TimeGenerated desc

External mailbox auto-forwarding rule creation (inbox rule / mailbox forwarding) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts per-mailbox forwarding persistence adjacent to UNC6508's rule-based exfiltration: creation of an inbox rule or mailbox setting that forwards/redirects mail to an external recipient. Complements the org-level transport-rule UC by covering the per-user forwarding pivot. Rationale: The article centers on rule-based mail theft; the reviewer flagged per-mailbox forwarding as the adjacent persistence pivot. Mapped to M365 New-InboxRule/Set-Mailbox forwarding params (native Workspace equivalent = Gmail auto-forwarding setting). Distinct log shape from the org-level transport-rule UC. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/prc-targets-us-medical-research
ATT&CKT1114.003 T1098.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User legitimately forwarding their mail to a personal/secondary corporate account during leave
  • Helpdesk configuring forwarding for a departing employee's mailbox
  • Shared-mailbox to ticketing-system forwarding (e.g. support@ to a SaaS desk)
  • Mailbox migration tooling setting temporary forwarding during cutover
Suppression filter
| where ForwardTarget !has "@yourorg.com" and ForwardTarget !has_any ("support@","helpdesk@","tickets@")
Response runbook
1) Triage: check whether ForwardTarget is external/free-mail and whether the creating principal differs from the mailbox owner (delegate-set forwarding is higher risk). 2) Contain: remove the forwarding rule, reset the owner's credentials and the setter's if different, and revoke sessions. 3) Hunt: enumerate all forwarding rules tenant-wide, correlate with any logon from 23.169.65.49, and check for transport-rule BCCs and mailbox-access fan-out by the same principal.

| order by Timestamp desc

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/20
tags:
  - attack.t1114.003
  - attack.t1098.002
logsource:
  product: m365
  service: exchange
detection:
  selection:
    Operation:
      - 'New-InboxRule'
      - 'Set-InboxRule'
      - 'Set-Mailbox'
    Parameters|contains:
      - 'ForwardTo'
      - 'RedirectTo'
      - 'ForwardingSmtpAddress'
  condition: selection
level: medium
Single principal accessing many distinct mailboxes within one hour AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the post-compromise mailbox-access fan-out implied by UNC6508 reaching many high-value research/defense mailboxes after gaining admin/domain rights. Flags one principal (delegate, admin, or service account) reading 10+ distinct mailboxes in a 1-hour window — a precursor to setting up rule-based collection at scale. Rationale: The article describes targeting of many high-value research/defense mailboxes after admin compromise; reviewer suggestion #5 frames this as a credential-access fan-out. Threshold/aggregation logic (dcount per principal per hour) — Sigma omitted as it is not single-event-shape. M365 MailItemsAccessed is the closest available analog to Workspace bulk mailbox access. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/prc-targets-us-medical-research • https://www.theregister.com/research/2026/06/15/google-says-prc-linked-spies-hid-in-medical-research-networks-for-more-than-a-year/5254547
ATT&CKT1114.002 T1078.004
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • eDiscovery / legal-hold tooling enumerating mailboxes under a service account
  • Backup or archiving solution (e.g. Veeam, Barracuda) reading many mailboxes on a schedule
  • Helpdesk admin doing legitimate bulk mailbox troubleshooting
  • Mail-migration service account during a tenant migration window
Suppression filter
| where UserId !has_any ("svc-ediscovery","svc-backup","veeam","migration") and AccountDisplayName !has_any ("eDiscovery","Backup","Migration")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the principal and whether it is a known service/backup/eDiscovery account; check the source IP(s) and whether access pattern is scheduled/uniform (tooling) vs bursty/interactive (suspicious). 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, disable the account, revoke tokens/sessions, and reset credentials. 3) Hunt: pivot to any forwarding/transport rules created by this principal afterward, correlate logons with 23.169.65.49 and impossible-travel, and review which mailboxes were touched for sensitivity.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "MailItemsAccessed"
| where isnotempty(ObjectName)
| summarize DistinctMailboxes = dcount(ObjectName), Mailboxes = make_set(ObjectName, 50), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 20) by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where DistinctMailboxes >= 10   // 10+ distinct mailboxes/hr by one principal = fan-out (reviewer threshold)
| order by DistinctMailboxes desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Operation == "MailItemsAccessed"
| where isnotempty(MailboxOwnerUPN) and UserId != MailboxOwnerUPN   // cross-mailbox (delegate/admin) access only
| summarize DistinctMailboxes = dcount(MailboxOwnerUPN), Mailboxes = make_set(MailboxOwnerUPN, 50), IPs = make_set(ClientIP, 20) by UserId, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DistinctMailboxes >= 10   // 10+ distinct mailboxes/hr by one principal = fan-out (reviewer threshold)
| order by DistinctMailboxes desc
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\winword.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\excel.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\powerpnt.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\outlook.exe"

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

detection:

NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Overlord/VSIX stealer staging ZIP exfil to campaign C2 from a developer-tool process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process
VS Code/Cursor 'runOn folderOpen' tasks.json auto-execution spawning a script interpreter AIExploitation High
Hunts the signature UNK_DeadDrop/Contagious Interview primitive: a cloned 'coding assignment' repo ships a hidden .vscode/tasks.json that abuses VS Code's and Cursor's runOn:folderOpen task automation to execute a loader the instant the folder is opened, with no user interaction. Detects Code.exe / Cursor.exe spawning a script host (wscript/cscript/powershell/bash/sh), which is anomalous for the editor process itself. Rationale: Anchored on the article's explicit 'runOn folderOpen' technique in .vscode/tasks.json executing on folder open in VS Code/Cursor; the editor process spawning wscript/cscript (the named Windows VBScript loader) is the high-fidelity discriminator. Cross-checked Proofpoint UNK_DeadDrop write-up and CyberSecurityNews. Cross-checked against: • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/dont-fear-repo-unkdeaddrop-phishing-campaign-targets-developers-steal • https://cybersecuritynews.com/north-korea-aligned-hackers-abuse-github-repositories/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059.005 T1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer using the VS Code integrated terminal to launch PowerShell/bash manually
  • A legitimate workspace tasks.json that runs a PowerShell build/lint step on folder open
  • WSL/Git-Bash integrations spawning bash.exe from Code.exe
  • Extension-driven shells (e.g. a test runner that shells out)
  • Cursor AI agent executing an approved terminal command
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildCmd has_any ("build","npm run","tsc","eslint","pytest","jest") and Editor == "Code.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full tasks.json from the opened workspace and the child process command line; confirm whether a 'runOn':'folderOpen' task exists and what it executes. Check repo origin (was it git-cloned from an emailed GitHub link in the last 24h?). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the loader and any child wscript/cscript/node tree, and quarantine the cloned repo folder. 3) Hunt: check DeviceNetworkEvents on that host for 23.137.105.75:5173 and the other campaign IPs, look for VSIX sideloads (--install-extension) and browser wallet/credential file reads, and search the org for the same repo URL across mailboxes.

| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Editor=InitiatingProcessFileName, EditorCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Child=FileName, ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("Code.exe","Cursor.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","mshta.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

UNK_DeadDrop Windows loader: VBScript/CMD chain sideloading a named malicious Jupyter VSIX AIInstallation High
Detects the Windows infection chain where a VBScript loader runs a CMD file that installs a malicious VS Code extension (VSIX) masquerading as a Jupyter/Google productivity tool. Keys on the three Yeeth-Security-named extensions and on the 'code --install-extension' sideload of a local .vsix file driven by a script-host parent — a combination that does not occur in benign extension installs from the Marketplace UI. Rationale: Uses the three exact malicious VSIX names from Yeeth Security (ByteBinTools.jupyter-powerdev-2026.6.8, ToolCraft.jupyter-powertools-3.21.0, OLDev.markdown-mode-devtools-2.1.0) plus the local-VSIX sideload pattern (--install-extension <file>.vsix) the loader uses — neither occurs in normal Marketplace installs. Corroborated via The Hacker News reporting on the Yeeth Security findings. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/north-korean-hackers-are-turning.html • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/dont-fear-repo-unkdeaddrop-phishing-campaign-targets-developers-steal
ATT&CKT1059.005 T1059.003 T1176
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal CI/CD that sideloads pinned internal .vsix files via 'code --install-extension'
  • A developer manually installing a vetted local extension build during testing
  • Air-gapped/offline extension distribution workflows that install VSIX from a share
  • Security team detonation/sandbox of the IOC for analysis
Suppression filter
| where not (ParentCmd has_any ("azure-pipelines","jenkins","\\ci\\","buildagent") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the extension name matches one of the three IOCs or is an unsanctioned local VSIX; enumerate %USERPROFILE%\.vscode\extensions for the publisher folders (ByteBinTools/ToolCraft/OLDev). 2) Contain: uninstall/quarantine the extension folder, isolate the host, and revoke any cloud/dev credentials reachable from that user. 3) Hunt: check for the VBScript/CMD parent chain, outbound to 23.137.105.75:5173, SharePoint/Microsoft Graph API C2 traffic (Graph token use by node.exe), and the same VSIX across other developer endpoints.

| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("jupyter-powerdev","jupyter-powertools","markdown-mode-devtools","ByteBinTools","ToolCraft.jupyter","OLDev.markdown")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "--install-extension" and ProcessCommandLine has ".vsix")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, Parent=InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has_any ("jupyter-powerdev","jupyter-powertools","markdown-mode-devtools","ByteBinTools","ToolCraft.jupyter","OLDev.markdown")

| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

UNK_DeadDrop C2 egress to 23.137.105[.]75:5173 and related campaign IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Network IOC detection for the UNK_DeadDrop exfiltration server. The Windows pipeline POSTs harvested ZIPs to 23.137.105[.]75 on TCP/5173 then terminates; Linux/macOS Overlord agents beacon to the same and adjacent infrastructure. Any outbound connection to these confirmed IPs (with 5173 as the documented port) is high-confidence campaign activity. Rationale: Pre-extracted, article-named C2/exfil IPs (23.137.105.75 with the documented POST port 5173, plus 170.205.29.83 and 170.205.30.227). The article explicitly states the Windows pipeline uploads ZIPs to 23.137.105.75:5173. Projecting InitiatingProcess surfaces the responsible binary for triage without a placeholder pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/north-korean-hackers-are-turning.html • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/dont-fear-repo-unkdeaddrop-phishing-campaign-targets-developers-steal
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel feed scanners or honeyclients deliberately touching the IOC IP
  • A security analyst sandbox detonating the sample
  • Shared-hosting IP reuse where a benign service later occupies the same address (validate WHOIS/age)
  • Internal proxy/IDS that mirrors/replays traffic to the IP for inspection
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess and user on the connecting host; confirm whether a recent GitHub repo clone or VSIX install preceded the beacon. 2) Contain: block the three IPs at egress/firewall, isolate the host, and capture the staged ZIP(s) from temp before they are cleaned up. 3) Hunt: pivot on the InitiatingProcess hash org-wide, look for the tasks.json/VBScript loader chain and browser-wallet file reads, and rotate any crypto-wallet/dev credentials accessed from the host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("23.137.105.75","170.205.29.83","170.205.30.227")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("23.137.105.75","170.205.29.83","170.205.30.227")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Contagious Interview Git hooks: .githooks/pre-commit firing a shell on repo clone/commit AIInstallation Medium
Detects the Contagious Interview shift to Git hook execution, where a cloned 'coding assessment' repo carries a .githooks/pre-commit that fires malicious code on first commit/clone. Keys on git.exe spawning a shell/script interpreter whose command line references .githooks or pre-commit — a behaviour distinct from normal IDE-driven git operations. Rationale: Anchored on the article's named persistence/trigger path '.githooks/pre-commit' that Contagious Interview now uses instead of .vscode/tasks.json or package.json. Requiring the .githooks/pre-commit token on the command line keeps it from firing on ordinary git activity. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/north-korean-hackers-are-turning.html
ATT&CKT1546 T1059 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate pre-commit framework (pre-commit.com) running linters/formatters via Python or node
  • Husky git hooks invoking node-based checks in JS projects
  • A monorepo with a custom .githooks directory configured via core.hooksPath
  • Developer running 'git commit' that triggers an approved local hook script
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildCmd has_any ("husky","pre-commit.com","lint-staged","prettier","black --","flake8"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the .githooks/pre-commit (and core.hooksPath config) in the repo; determine whether it executes a build/lint tool (benign) or fetches/decodes a payload (malicious). Check repo origin and clone time. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the hook-spawned process tree, and remove/quarantine the repo. 3) Hunt: look for follow-on C2 to the campaign IPs, VSIX sideloads, and the same repo cloned elsewhere; review the developer's own repos for injected commits (worm-like propagation).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("git.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","node.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".githooks" or ProcessCommandLine has "pre-commit" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has ".githooks"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Parent=InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Child=FileName, ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("git.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","node.exe")
| where CommandLine has ".githooks" or CommandLine has "pre-commit"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Named malicious Jupyter/Markdown VSIX extensions written to the VS Code extensions directory AIInstallation High
File-event detection for the three Yeeth-Security-identified malicious extensions landing in a user's VS Code extensions folder. Catches the install regardless of vector (Marketplace pull or local sideload) by matching the exact publisher.extension folder/file names under .vscode\extensions or .cursor\extensions. Rationale: Directly uses the three exact malicious extension identifiers (ByteBinTools.jupyter-powerdev-2026.6.8, ToolCraft.jupyter-powertools-3.21.0, OLDev.markdown-mode-devtools-2.1.0) from Yeeth Security. These strings are unique to the campaign, giving a very low FP rate. Cross-checked against The Hacker News coverage. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/north-korean-hackers-are-turning.html
ATT&CKT1176 T1505
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security tooling staging the IOC files for analysis/quarantine
  • EDR/AV writing the file to a quarantine path (matches on substring) — validate ActionType and folder
  • Backup software copying a previously-infected profile
  • Threat-hunt team intentionally restoring the sample on a sandbox host
Suppression filter
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified") and FolderPath has_any ("\\.vscode\\extensions","\\.cursor\\extensions")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the FolderPath is a live .vscode/.cursor extensions directory (not a quarantine/backup path) and identify the writing process and user. 2) Contain: remove the extension folder, isolate the host, terminate VS Code/Cursor and any node.exe child handling Graph/SharePoint C2, and revoke the user's M365/Graph tokens. 3) Hunt: search CloudAppEvents/Graph for SharePoint sites used as a command queue, look for the VBScript loader and outbound to 23.137.105.75:5173, and sweep all developer endpoints for the same extension IDs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has_any ("jupyter-powerdev","jupyter-powertools","markdown-mode-devtools","ByteBinTools.jupyter","ToolCraft.jupyter","OLDev.markdown")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("jupyter-powerdev","jupyter-powertools","markdown-mode-devtools","ByteBinTools.jupyter","ToolCraft.jupyter","OLDev.markdown")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

North Korea supply-chain packages: malicious npm/Packagist deps dropped into a project tree AIDelivery Medium
Detects on-disk presence/installation of the named malicious packages tied to the broader North Korean developer-targeting activity: npm redeem-onchain-sdk, nicegui, period-newline (Axios follow-up stealers) and the compromised Packagist package roberts/leads (PHP→JS loader to DEV#POPPER). Matches package directories under node_modules/ or vendor/ created by a package manager. Rationale: Uses the exact malicious package names/versions from the article (redeem-onchain-sdk@1.0.7, nicegui@0.1.4, period-newline@0.1.0, Packagist roberts/leads). Pathing to node_modules/vendor scopes it to actual installation rather than mention. Corroborated by SafeDep's redeem-onchain-sdk analysis and Google/GTIG's Axios UNC1069 attribution. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/redeem-onchain-sdk-polymarket-npm-malware/ • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/north-korea-threat-actor-targets-axios-npm-package • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/north-korean-hackers-are-turning.html
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer who legitimately depends on a same-named but unrelated package (validate version: malicious are redeem-onchain-sdk@1.0.7, nicegui@0.1.4, period-newline@0.1.0)
  • Offline npm cache/mirror restoring an old lockfile that still references the package
  • Security research clone of the malicious repo for analysis
  • CI artifact cache rehydrating node_modules from a poisoned lockfile
Suppression filter
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the package's package.json/composer.json and check for postinstall/install scripts and the pinned version against the IOC versions; identify which project lockfile pulled it. 2) Contain: remove the package, purge node_modules/vendor and the npm/composer cache, isolate the host, and rotate developer/cloud/crypto credentials reachable from the build. 3) Hunt: search for outbound stealer C2 from node/python, scan other repos/lockfiles in the org for the same dependency names, and review recent commits for injected dependency lines.

| where FolderPath has_any (@"\node_modules\redeem-onchain-sdk", "/node_modules/redeem-onchain-sdk", @"\node_modules\nicegui", "/node_modules/nicegui", @"\node_modules\period-newline", "/node_modules/period-newline", @"\vendor\roberts\leads", "/vendor/roberts/leads")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Overlord/VSIX stealer staging ZIP exfil to campaign C2 from a developer-tool process AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the credential/wallet-theft payoff stage: a developer-tooling process (node, Code/Cursor, python, or the script-host loader) opening an outbound connection to the campaign C2 — either the named IPs or the documented TCP/5173 to a public host. The article states the Windows pipeline uploads ZIPs of stolen browser-wallet/credential data then terminates, so process-attributed egress complements the pure IOC rule even if infrastructure rotates. Rationale: Combines the article's named C2 IPs and the explicit exfil port (5173) with the developer-tooling process set that performs the theft (node/Code/python/script-host), targeting the stated 'upload ZIPs then terminate' behaviour. Process attribution keeps signal if the IP rotates while public-only gating on 5173 avoids local Vite dev-server noise. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/north-korean-hackers-are-turning.html • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/dont-fear-repo-unkdeaddrop-phishing-campaign-targets-developers-steal
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1041 T1005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A local front-end dev server (Vite defaults to TCP/5173) reached over the internet via a tunnel/proxy — gate kept to public IPs reduces but won't eliminate
  • node/python build tooling legitimately POSTing telemetry to a 5173 cloud endpoint
  • A self-hosted internal service that happens to listen on 5173 behind a public IP
  • Security sandbox replaying the sample's C2
Suppression filter
| where not (RemotePort == 5173 and RemoteUrl has_any ("localhost","127.0.0.1"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process command line and whether stolen-data ZIPs were staged in temp/AppData before the connection; confirm the destination is not an internal/dev Vite server. 2) Contain: block the destination, isolate the host, and immediately rotate all browser-stored credentials and crypto-wallet seed/keys for the user. 3) Hunt: pull DeviceFileEvents for .zip writes by the same process and reads of browser 'Local Extension Settings'/wallet app data, then sweep for the loader chain and VSIX IOCs across other developer endpoints.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","Code.exe","Cursor.exe","python.exe","pythonw.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where RemoteIP in ("23.137.105.75","170.205.29.83","170.205.30.227")
   or (RemotePort == 5173 and RemoteIPType == "Public")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("23.137.105.75","170.205.29.83","170.205.30.227")
   or (DstPortNumber == 5173 and not(ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr)))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\Code.exe OR *\\Cursor.exe OR *\\python.exe OR *\\pythonw.exe OR *\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe) (@DestinationIp:(23.137.105.75 OR 170.205.29.83 OR 170.205.30.227) OR @DestinationPort:5173)
